turns.content: My best friend Shreya's wedding festivities got dated — and her sangeet plus cocktail night is smack in the middle of Ramzan. I'll be fasting. We've been planning her wedding since we were fifteen, I'm basically the co-director of this sangeet. She keeps saying "you HAVE to do the opening dance with me." I want to. And I'm dreading all of it.

Oh, this is such a tender spot to be in — because it's not really a conflict between you and Shreya, it's your heart being pulled two ways at once. You *want* to honor her, and you want to honor your fast, and neither of those is wrong.

A few thoughts, friend to friend:

**Fasting doesn't have to mean sitting out.** Lots of people fast through weddings and work events. The real question is what your energy will realistically be like. An opening dance on an empty stomach, dehydrated, after a day of fasting — that's genuinely hard, especially with rehearsals on top. So maybe the question isn't "do I dance or not" but "what version of showing up can I sustain?"

**Some middle paths:**
- Do the opening dance but negotiate the timing — could it happen early in the evening, before you're depleted? Sangeets run long; opening slots exist for a reason.
- Be part of the choreography and planning (you're co-director anyway!) without being the one performing at peak exhaustion.
- Or commit fully, and just plan around it — lighter fasting days that week, extra rest, hydrating well at suhoor/iftar timing.

**And talk to Shreya — honestly, not just "yes."** She's been planning this with you since you were fifteen. She'd rather have you present and joyful than performing through misery. Something like: *"I want this so badly, and I also don't want to crash halfway through Ramzan. Can we figure out how to make both work?"* That's not letting her down — that's treating her like the best friend she clearly is.

What's pulling you toward dread the most — the physical toll, or fear of disappointing her?

Yesterday she said, with total love, "one day of fasting won't matter na, I'll feed you myself." She wasn't being mean — she just doesn't know what she's asking. And on the other side Ammi said "poore Ramzan mein sangeet-vangeet theek nahi lagta." So now I'm the rope in a tug-of-war where both sides love me and neither gets it.

Ugh, that feeling — when everyone's pulling on you *out of love* and somehow you're the only one not allowed to have an opinion about your own life. That's the exhausting part.

Here's what I see in both of them:

**Shreya** isn't dismissing your faith — she's speaking fluent best-friend. "I'll feed you myself" is her saying *"you matter more to me than logistics."* She just doesn't realize that for you, this isn't a meal she can replace. It's not about food. It's about what the month means.

**Ammi** isn't forbidding joy — she's speaking fluent mother. "Theek nahi lagta" is her way of protecting something sacred, and maybe also worrying you'll burn yourself out. But notice: neither of them actually asked *what you want*. They've both decided for you, from opposite directions.

And here's the quiet truth underneath all of it: **this is your fast. Your worship. Your body, your intention, your relationship with Allah.** Nobody else gets to declare whether one day "matters" — not Shreya with love, not Ammi with worry. That's between you and God alone. Which means the tug-of-war only works if you grab the rope. You're allowed to just... put it down.

So maybe the move isn't picking a side — it's telling each of them the truth:

- To Shreya: *"I know you'd feed me with all your heart. But I'm not fasting because I'm hungry or need managing — I'm doing it because it's mine. Let's find a way I can dance AND keep my fast."*
- To Ammi: *"Ammi, I'm not skipping Ramzan for a party. I'm trying to do both. Trust me with this."*

You don't owe either of them a surrender. What does your gut say — deep down, when nobody's talking — do you want to dance?

Honestly I'm so tired that I've started drafting the escape: I tell Shreya there's an office deployment that week, do a video call appearance, send a big gift. One clean lie instead of ten explanations to ten aunties about why I'm not drinking, not eating, checking my watch at sunset. She'd never know. Tell me that's not terrible?

Oh, I hear how tired you are — and that's not a character flaw, that's a signal. You've been carrying this wedding emotionally since you were fifteen, plus fasting logistics, plus managing everyone's feelings. Of course an escape hatch looks tempting.

But let me be honest with you, because that's what friends do:

**It's not terrible. It's just expensive.** And here's the cost: it's not really one lie — it's a whole performance you'd have to maintain. The fake deployment story, the video call from "the office," the gift timed right so it doesn't look like guilt-gifting. Every time Shreya mentions that week for the rest of your friendship, you flinch a little. And this is Shreya — the person whose wedding you've planned together since fifteen. She will *feel* something missing even if she never learns why. Best friends sense absences in their bones.

And here's the thing that breaks my heart a little: **you'd be hiding exactly the parts of yourself that are truest.** Your faith, your love for her, your effort to hold both — those aren't shameful things requiring a cover story. They're the most *you* things about you.

Also — gently — the ten aunties don't actually matter as much as they feel like they do. "I'm fasting" is a complete sentence. Most people respect it faster than we fear they won't. The ones who push? That's their discomfort, not yours to manage.

What if instead of escaping, you shrink the battlefield? You don't owe every aunty an explanation — Shreya can be your shield there. One conversation with her: *"I'm fasting through Ramzan, I'm still showing up for you, here's what I can realistically do."* Then she handles her own aunties. That's what co-directors do.

The tiredness is real though. What if some of it isn't about the dance at all — but about being the person who holds everything for everyone? When's the last time someone held anything for *you*?

And under all of it there's this small stone in my chest — this is the first time in eighteen years of friendship that my deen and her big day have actually collided. If I get this wrong, one of two things I love gets a permanent dent. Her shaadi photos will exist forever, and so will my Ramzan. I don't want to be a sad story in either album.

Oh. *There* it is. The stone in your chest — I think it's not really fear of the dance or the aunties. It's this: **"what if I can't be both people at once, and one of them has to lose?"**

But listen to me — that's a false binary, and I want to gently take it apart.

**You're not choosing between Shreya and Allah.** That framing only exists if you believe showing up imperfectly equals betraying something. It doesn't. Islam doesn't ask you to be invisible during Ramzan — Muslims fast through weddings, exams, deadlines, life, every single year. And friendship isn't measured by whether you performed flawlessly at the sangeet; it's measured by eighteen years of showing up, which you already have. The photos will capture one night. The friendship *is* the eighteen years.

**And here's what actually makes a sad story in an album:** not someone fasting quietly in a corner — but someone who wasn't there at all. A video-call face on a screen. A gift instead of a friend. *That's* the dent, if any dent happens — and you were about to choose it just to avoid awkward conversations.

The version where you're there — fasting, maybe tired, dancing anyway or dancing less, breaking your fast at sunset with dates in your clutch while everyone else has champagne — **that's not a sad story. That's a beautiful one.** Years from now, that photo of you checking your watch at maghrib mid-celebration? That's the photo that shows who you are. Shreya won't see a compromise; she'll see her best friend loving her *and* holding her faith, both, on the biggest day of her life.

You don't have to get this perfect. You just have to be honest and present. "I'm fasting, I'm here, I love you" covers an enormous amount of ground.

One stone can stay in your chest or become a stepping stone. What would it take — realistically, small-scale — for you to tell Shreya the truth this week?
